blocks.text: An adult carries about five litres of blood, and every drop completes a full circuit of the body roughly once a minute. In that single minute it delivers oxygen, collects carbon dioxide, carries hormones, fights bacteria and helps hold body temperature steady. No other tissue does so many jobs at once.

blocks.markdown:
## What blood is made of

Blood is a tissue: about 55% liquid **plasma** and 45% cells suspended in it.

**Plasma** is roughly 90% water. Dissolved in it are digested food (glucose, amino acids), excretory products (urea, carbon dioxide as hydrogencarbonate), hormones, mineral salts, and plasma proteins including fibrinogen and antibodies. Plasma without the clotting factors is called serum.

There are three kinds of blood cell, and picturing them helps. A **red blood cell** is a tiny biconcave disc — thinner in the middle than at the edges — with no nucleus and packed with the red pigment haemoglobin. A **white blood cell** is larger, irregular, and always has a nucleus. **Platelets** are not whole cells at all but small fragments of cytoplasm.

blocks.caption: Blood components and their functions

blocks.markdown:
### Why the red blood cell has that shape

Every feature of a red blood cell serves oxygen transport. It has **no nucleus**, leaving more room for haemoglobin. It is **biconcave**, which gives a larger surface area for a given volume so oxygen diffuses in and out faster. It is **tiny and flexible**, so it can squeeze single file through capillaries narrower than itself, passing very close to the tissues it serves.

In the lungs, where oxygen is plentiful, haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form bright red **oxyhaemoglobin**. In respiring tissues, where oxygen is scarce, the reaction reverses and oxygen is released. Most carbon dioxide travels a different route — dissolved in the plasma as hydrogencarbonate ions.

blocks.title: Carbon monoxide
blocks.text: Carbon monoxide from a generator or charcoal stove binds to haemoglobin about 250 times more strongly than oxygen, and the bond is almost irreversible. The blood is then unable to carry oxygen, which is why running a generator inside a closed room can kill.

blocks.markdown:
### Blood clotting

When a blood vessel is cut, platelets stick to the damaged surface and release an enzyme, **thrombokinase**. In the presence of calcium ions and vitamin K this converts the inactive plasma protein **prothrombin** into active **thrombin**. Thrombin then converts soluble **fibrinogen** into insoluble threads of **fibrin**, which form a mesh that traps blood cells and hardens into a clot.

The clot seals the wound, stops further blood loss and keeps bacteria out while the tissue heals. Anyone lacking a clotting factor — as in haemophilia — bleeds dangerously from a small cut.

### Blood groups and transfusion

Red blood cells carry surface markers called **antigens** (A and B), and plasma may carry **antibodies** (anti-A and anti-B). If a donor's antigen meets the matching antibody in the recipient's plasma the cells clump together — **agglutination** — which can block vessels and kill the patient.

blocks.caption: The ABO system. Group O is the universal donor because its cells carry no antigen; group AB is the universal recipient because its plasma carries no antibody.

blocks.title: Deciding whether a transfusion is safe
blocks.prompt: A patient of blood group A rhesus negative needs blood urgently. The blood bank has units of group B positive, group O negative and group AB positive. Which unit should be given, and why must the others be refused?

steps.text: List the recipient's antibodies. Group A plasma contains anti-B antibodies, and being rhesus negative the patient has no rhesus antigen.
Test the group B unit. Its cells carry antigen B, which the recipient's anti-B would attack, causing agglutination. Refuse it.
Test the group AB unit. Its cells carry both A and B antigens, so anti-B would again cause agglutination. Refuse it.
Test the group O negative unit. Its cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so the recipient's anti-A and anti-B have nothing to attack.

Check the rhesus factor. A rhesus negative patient must not receive rhesus positive blood, because they would form anti-rhesus antibodies that endanger any later transfusion or pregnancy. The O unit is negative, so it is safe.

blocks.answer: Give the group O rhesus negative unit. The B and AB units would be agglutinated by the recipient's anti-B antibodies, and any rhesus positive unit would stimulate the formation of anti-rhesus antibodies.

blocks.title: Antigen on the cell, antibody in the plasma
blocks.text: Almost every mistake in transfusion questions comes from mixing these up. Antigens are on the donor's red cells; antibodies are in the recipient's plasma. Ask only one question: does the recipient have an antibody against any antigen the donor's cells carry?

points: Blood is plasma plus red cells, white cells and platelets.
Red cells have no nucleus and are biconcave, which maximises haemoglobin content and surface area for oxygen transport.
Phagocytes engulf bacteria while lymphocytes make antibodies.
Clotting converts fibrinogen to fibrin threads through the action of thrombin, and needs calcium and vitamin K.
Group O is the universal donor and group AB the universal recipient; agglutination occurs when a donor antigen meets the matching recipient antibody.
